title: The Tea That Costs You Something

blocks.p: The tea was genmaicha, green tea mixed with grains of toasted rice. It is the cheap, everyday tea of Japanese kitchens, the kind that smells a little like popcorn. It was the most dangerous thing Rei had drunk all week, because it was so ordinary. Kishin understood that the way to a guarded person is not through fear. It is through the small kindness that person has been too busy to receive. Rinka poured and asked, in the host's gentle voice, whether he had eaten. Whether he was sleeping. Whether the heat was keeping him up. Each question landed in the part of him that no one had asked about since the fourteenth, the night Gin went quiet. That part of him had been holding his brother's vanishing alone, in a city of nine million. He had to set the cup down so his hand would not give him away.

This was what it wanted, and it was never money. It wanted him to be comfortable near it. Comfort was how the wearing-down got in, one warm hour at a time. Then one day a person would find they could not think a hard thought about Kanna-sensei without feeling a small grief at their own disloyalty.
Rei made himself ask the only question worth the climb. Who drew the battery down?

Rinka answered without games, because Kishin gained nothing by hiding it and everything by being the one who told him. "Both," she said. "The Healer comes for it gently, in the small hours. What he takes, he uses to soften the seams in Kita so they will part without tearing. A surgeon thinning a wall into a membrane he can lift clean. And the boy who preaches draws for me, in great greedy pulls, because I do not want the wall lifted. I want it broken. The held breath let out all at once." She poured more tea he had not asked for. "The Healer thinks he steals from me. I let him. A thief who drinks from my cup is a thief I can always find." She let the next part land softly. "And lately the grief has been coming faster. Two of us pulling at the same harvest is very good for the harvest."
"He's hunting you," Rei said. It was a guess, and it was right.

"He means to kill me." She said it the way people mention rain. "A demon can only be killed on this side from inside a body. That is what your brother is to him, you understand. A hand to do it with." The kind eyes rested on him. "It is a door I have not yet had to close. There is time."
Rei read the room while she spoke, and the thing in her did not seem to mind being read. He did not think it was afraid. He thought, quietly, that it should be.

And there it was, the thing he had climbed the stairs without knowing he needed. His brother's captor and the cult's god were not two separate horrors. They were two ends of one rope, and the rope was being paid out from this room. He should have felt the satisfaction of a case coming together. Instead he felt the warm cup in his hands, and Rinka's patient eyes on him, and the terrible peace of the moment, like a family kitchen at night. He had already begun to owe her. Not for a service. For a comfort he had accepted. The bill for comfort is the hardest bill to read, because it never arrives as a number. It arrives as a new softness, in the exact place where a person used to keep his edge.

Around them the circle was ending. People stretched their legs and murmured to each other. Somebody slid a window open behind the white paper, and the night came in. Rei heard the cicadas in a garden below, a motorbike far off, and the small bell of the last streetcar going down toward Ōji. After the ringing silence of the circle, the ordinary noise sounded almost rude. An older woman in an apron moved round the ring with a lacquered wooden box, and each person laid an envelope in it with a name written on the front. She carried the box to a cupboard, locked it and hung the key on a cord round her neck. Then she checked the clock against a handwritten timetable taped inside the cupboard door and wrote something on it.

blocks.cap: The circle's Keeper, who holds the money, the room and the schedule

blocks.p: "Our Keeper," Rinka said, following his eyes. "She keeps the house. The money, the room, the schedule, the photographs on the wall. Without her none of this would stand up for a week."

Gin had a line for that too. A cult can survive losing its Voice. It rarely survives losing its Keeper, because the Keeper holds the daily work of tending it. Rei looked at the woman in the apron, at her tired, careful hands. He understood that she believed she was doing the most loving thing she had ever done.

He let his reading go outward through the building. Gin's chapter sorted a cult's people into layers, and Rei could see every layer from here. The ring kneeling here tonight were the Faithful. They knew there was a presence. They served it and brought the offerings, and they had come far enough to be locked in. Below them, spread across the ward, were the people who never climbed the humming stairs at all. They went to the weekly letting-go circles in borrowed municipal rooms, the grief meetings with free tea and paper tissues. Gin called that outer ring the Unknowing. They were the cover, the numbers and the place where new members were found. And the thing at the centre took a thin, low feeding from every one of those rooms without anyone noticing.
"And your Voice?" Rei asked. "Who does it speak through, out there?"

"Our Voice is in the city tonight," Rinka said. "In a drained pool, with forty people who love him." She meant Kaito. Gin had written that the Voice is often a real medium, and the most completely deceived person in the room. Rei thought of the courier preaching in the dead hour. He was not sure Kaito was deceived any longer. He thought Kaito might simply be empty.
"And the one who saw it first? The one it all started with?"

Rinka touched her own chest, lightly, over the river stone. "The first to see the far shore," she said. "She is with us still. In spirit." Gin had a word for that person as well. The Touched. The Touched is the one whose first experience of the veil the whole doctrine is built around. Sometimes the Touched and the Voice are the same person. Sometimes the Touched is dead, and the cult is built on the memory of what happened to her. Rei looked at the stone and did not reach for it again.

The rites were laid out in front of him if he chose to see them. A rite is any act a group repeats to bind itself to what it serves, and Gin's chapter listed them in order. The naming came first, when the ring first called the presence the Far Shore and spoke of it as a being owed devotion. Then the offering, the envelopes in the lacquered box, the names of the dead given every week. Then the proof, the cold shimmer at the centre, the moment each mourner heard a loved voice in their ear exactly when doubt would have come. And somewhere past those, kept private, was the binding rite. Gin said that whoever found a group's binding rite had found the exact line between its victims and its participants.

Rei asked what the answer would cost, because he would not leave owing a thing he could not see. He had watched what unseen debts did to the people in his brother's ledger. Kishin smiled through Rinka's mouth and told him the price, in the only currency it kept.

It did not want his blood or his service or his soul. Those were merchants' words, for merchants' appetites. It wanted the next grief he carried to come here first. Not all his grief. Just the next fresh one, whenever it landed, before he had decided alone what to do with it. The way the man from Sumida had brought his. The way the widow had brought hers. He would bring it here while it was still warm, kneel in the eastern seat, and let the room take its weight off him for one evening. Then the knowledge he had bought tonight would be paid in full. It was, she pointed out gently, the same agreement everyone in the ring had made. And look how lightly they carried their losses now.
So that was the binding rite. Not a blade or an oath. A seat on the eastern side and one evening's relief.

blocks.cap: A circle of chairs, the funnel that draws people down

blocks.p: Rei traced it then, the way he would trace a poisoning, using the widow who had whispered to him. Gin had walked backwards through the funnel with enough former members to draw it. It was the same shape almost every time. First the hook. A real experience of the veil. Her husband's voice in the tide at the seawall, a thing that had truly happened to her, and nobody can argue a person out of a thing that truly happened. Then the meeting. Someone who did not tell her she had imagined it. Someone who took both her hands and said, "I know what that was, and you are not alone, and there are others." The validation is the recruitment, Gin had written. Everything after it is detail. Then the frame. A name for the experience, a doctrine, the far shore where the dead wait, and a being at the centre who could reach them and was owed something for it. Then the deepening. Come once. Come weekly. Bring a name in an envelope. Stop seeing the sister who said this was not healthy. A flat demand would be refused. A gentle slope is walked down. And last the lock. The thing that cannot be taken back. The eastern seat.
No one joins, Gin had written under his drawing of it. People are drawn down.

And then, because he was honest, Rei ran the same funnel on himself. The hook was the kitchen at 3:47 in the morning, and a brother gone. The meeting was tonight, a voice asking if he had eaten. The frame was being told he was expected, that his name was already in her book. The deepening was a second cup of tea. The lock was the price on the table.

He thought of Gin. He thought of the grief he had carried up these stairs and would carry down them, the one with his brother's name on it. It was still unspent, and still his. It was the only thing keeping him walking toward Gin while the whole city walked away. In its perfect hospitality, Kishin had asked for the one grief that must never be soothed. The day Rei stopped hurting over Gin would be the day he stopped coming for him. The demon knew this. That was the cleverness of the price. It had not asked him to betray his brother. It had asked him to be comforted about him. It trusted that he was tired enough, after a week of this heat and this dread and this loneliness, to want comfort more than he wanted the edge that comfort would cost.
"You keep your word, I suppose," Rei said.

"Always." Rinka tilted her head. "I am not like your brother's thief, who signs forms for the privilege of being trusted. Or the little contracted one in Kōenji, who keeps his Usami like a houseplant and waters him every morning." The smile did not change. "I did not keep Fukai like that. There was no need."

Rei had read that name on a train only days ago, in pencil, down the margin of a CVD card. Ren, the demon in the Vessel Program, kept what was left of Usami. Kishin had kept nothing of Rinka at all. It had turned the lights out one by one, and it wanted him to know it had felt nothing while it did.

Rinka set the iron pot down with a soft iron sound. Around them the congregation was gathering their sandals and saying goodnight. They were ordinary people, stepping out into the Obon dark a little lighter than they had come. Not one of them looked back at the centre that had carried them. Rei could leave the same way. He could take everything he had learned tonight and owe nothing but the next ache. Surely the next ache was months away. Surely he would be stronger by then. That was exactly the size of lie this room was built to make feel like sense.

He stood up. He did not say yes. He did not say no, either, because he did not trust his voice to stay his own. The tea had gone cold in his hands, and he had not noticed it cooling. That, he thought, was the whole lesson.
He was at the door, one hand on the frame, when she spoke again. She did not raise her voice. She never needed to.
"Saturday, Rei-kun," Kanna-sensei said. "Bring whatever you are carrying by then. The eastern seat will be warm."

Kun is the friendly ending people put on a boy's name, the way a teacher speaks to a favourite pupil. Rei went down the humming stairs past the child's sandals, and he did not let himself count how many days were left until Saturday.
